title: OOP
intro: Object-oriented programming groups related state and behavior so complex programs stay understandable. In Python, classes are most useful when a concept has data that changes over time plus operations that belong to that data. This topic teaches you how classes, instances, methods, and composition work in real code, and when a plain function is still the better choice.
mental_model: A class defines a type of object. Each instance carries its own state, and methods operate on that state through `self`. Prefer small classes with clear responsibility. Use composition to combine objects, and use inheritance only when an `is-a` relationship is truly meaningful.
must_know: `__init__` initializes instance state for each new object.
`self` refers to the current instance inside instance methods.
Class variables are shared across instances; instance variables are per-object.
Composition is usually simpler than deep inheritance trees.
Dataclasses reduce boilerplate for classes that mostly hold data.
common_traps: Accidentally storing instance state as class variables.
Overusing inheritance for code reuse that composition could handle more clearly.
Creating classes for trivial one-step transformations better handled by functions.
Putting too many unrelated responsibilities in one class.
interview: Explain the difference between class variables and instance variables.
Explain when to choose composition over inheritance.
Show a small class that encapsulates state plus behavior.
Use clear examples for `__init__`, instance methods, and object lifecycle.
real_world: Service monitoring code often models service state, health checks, and retry policies as classes so behavior stays close to the data it modifies.
API SDK clients commonly use small classes for auth config, request builders, and response parsing helpers.
outcome: By the end of this topic, you should be able to design and implement small classes with clear responsibilities, distinguish shared versus per-instance state, and decide when OOP improves code clarity.

lesson_sections.title: 1. Class Definitions and Instance Creation
lesson_sections.body: A class defines attributes and methods for objects of that type. Calling the class creates an instance. Treat class definitions as domain modeling tools: each class should represent a concept with a clear responsibility.

lesson_sections.title: 2. __init__, Instance State, and self
lesson_sections.body: `__init__` sets up per-instance state. Inside instance methods, `self` points to the current object. Understanding this is essential for avoiding shared-state bugs and writing predictable methods.

lesson_sections.title: 3. Class Variables vs Instance Variables
lesson_sections.body: Class variables are shared across all instances, while instance variables belong to each object. Mixing them up can cause subtle bugs where one object's change affects every object unexpectedly.
lesson_sections.source_label: Python Tutorial: Class and Instance Variables

lesson_sections.title: 4. Methods, Encapsulation, and API Shape
lesson_sections.body: Methods should expose a clean interface and keep object internals manageable. Encapsulation does not mean hiding everything; it means presenting operations that keep object state valid and understandable.

lesson_sections.title: 5. Inheritance vs Composition
lesson_sections.body: Inheritance is useful when subclasses genuinely specialize a base class contract. Composition is usually safer for assembling behavior from smaller pieces. Start with composition unless inheritance expresses a natural relationship.

lesson_sections.title: 6. Dataclasses for Data-Centric Models
lesson_sections.body: When a class mainly stores structured data, dataclasses reduce boilerplate while preserving clarity. They are especially useful for configuration and record-like objects that still benefit from type hints and defaults.
